Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

articles.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
articles.snippet: Ukrainian forces are fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet tunnel in the Kharkiv region.
articles.full_text:
Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
- Published
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work â with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".
There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.
It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

articles.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
articles.snippet: The three leaders will meet together for the first time on Thursday during a closely-watched summit.
articles.full_text:
Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
- Published
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.
The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.
After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.
Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.
However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.
A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.
Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.
It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.
Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".
In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.
Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".
Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.
The south-east Chinese city the Apec summit is being held in is a booming area for manufacturing and advanced tech.
It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.
Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.
Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.
Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

articles.title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
articles.snippet: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which has also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize
articles.full_text:
William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to reflect on the enduring ties between the UK and India, as they wrapped up their three-day visit to the country.
William and Catherine arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official overseas trip together in four years.
The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.
It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.
A Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UKâIndia bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".
The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and added how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.
Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the India-UK partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".
The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.
When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
The royal spokesperson said that the meeting touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.
The first engagement of their visit saw them play street cricket in Mumbai alongside cricket star Sachin Tendulkar, who holds the record for being the highest run scorer in international cricket.
William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.
As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.
And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

articles.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
articles.snippet: Bahrain says it was also attacked by Iran following a US air strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Gulf on Tuesday.
articles.full_text:
Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
- Published
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.
The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
- Published16 hours ago
Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
- Published3 days ago
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.
The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".
"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.
Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.
On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.
In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".
At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
articles.snippet: Critics have their say as to whether GTA 6, the most anticipated video game of all time, lives up to the hype.
articles.full_text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
- Published
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (Â£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
Early nominations
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.
It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.
The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.
The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.
Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.
There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."
It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.
Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

articles.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
articles.snippet: Inass Touloub's body was found along the A10 road in 1987, bearing marks of abuse, and was not identified until 2018.
articles.full_text:
Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France in 1987
- Published
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.
The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.
Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in SuÃ¨vres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.
She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".
Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother â tested in an unrelated case â matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.
The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.
During the trial, prosecutor AnaÃ¯s Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.
The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.
French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.
El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.
Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

articles.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
articles.snippet: The purchase has sparked outrage over its cost as many Ghanaians struggle with rising cost of living.
articles.full_text:
Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (Â£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations?
- Published7 January 2025
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (Â£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.
"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.
Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

articles.title: Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge

articles.snippet: An Israeli court extended the detention of Abu Safia nearly two years after Israel's army detained him.
articles.full_text:
Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release.
Abu Safia’s lawyer said that a court in Beersheba decided on Wednesday to extend the physician’s detention for a further six months, according to Abu Safia’s account on X.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Israeli rights group raises concerns about jailed doctor amid Gaza strikes
- list 3 of 3‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare
The court said that Abu Safia “poses a threat to the State of Israel”, his lawyer reported.
“Dr Hussam questioned why his detention order was being renewed once again, expressing that he is being punished for fulfilling his humanitarian mission and professional duty as a doctor at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza,” the social media post added.
The Israeli army detained Abu Safia in December 2024, along with other staff members and patients, during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza.
International agencies and rights groups have called for the physician’s release on multiple occasions, highlighting reports that he is being subjected to abuse in detention.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said in July that Israel “must immediately release Dr Abu Safiya, or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offence and grant him a fair trial”.
OHCHR added that it received information indicating Abu Safia “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care”.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said last week it had obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a significant loss of weight, a drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated.
“Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said.

articles.title: What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Billions have been pledged for Gaza since a 2025 'ceasefire', but rebuilding hasn’t begun and Israeli attacks continue.
articles.full_text:
What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?
Billions have been pledged for Gaza since an October 2025 ‘ceasefire’, but rebuilding has not begun, and Israeli attacks continue.
Donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza through US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. But more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin, and nearly 1.4 million Palestinians are still living in makeshift shelters.
Even preliminary reconstruction efforts have stalled. The board had asked for $280m to fund the initial building phase, but in September it said most of that money remained unspent.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action
- list 2 of 3Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way
- list 3 of 3Palestinians find refuge in ancient caves after Israel demolishes homes
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board warned that the truce between Israel and Hamas could collapse unless immediate steps are taken to carry out the ceasefire deal, according to The Associated Press.
The next day, on Wednesday, Israel began its first major military ground operation in the Gaza Strip since the ceasefire began, attacking refugee camps in the central part of the enclave.
Since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,658 Palestinians and injured 6,000, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Israel continues to block the entry of 60,000 mobile homes promised under the ceasefire deal and to severely restrict food and medical aid into the besieged enclave. It has also yet to allow the Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza to enter the Strip.
What is the Board of Peace?
United States President Trump proposed the board in September 2025 as part of his 20-point plan for Gaza.
On November 17, 2025, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, which recognised the board as a transitional administration responsible for setting the framework and coordinating funding for Gaza’s redevelopment.
The resolution authorises its role in Gaza until December 31, 2027, unless the UN Security Council decides otherwise. The board’s charter also allows it to work in other areas affected by conflict.
Trump chairs the board and can only be replaced if he resigns or is unable to serve. He also represents the US.
He appoints its executive board, whose members are Ajay Banga, Tony Blair, Martin Edelman, Robert Gabriel Jr, Jared Kushner, Marc Rowan, Marco Rubio, Steve Witkoff, and Susie Wiles.
Each member state has one vote. Decisions need a majority of those present and voting, and Trump’s approval. He can also veto executive board decisions.
Under the plan, Palestinian technocrats would run Gaza’s day-to-day affairs through the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, led by Ali Shaath. The committee reports to the board, but Israel has not allowed it to enter Gaza, and it operates from Cairo.
The board has 28 members: Albania, Argentina, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Belarus, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Egypt, El Salvador, Hungary, Indonesia, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Mongolia, Morocco, Pakistan, Paraguay, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam.
Germany, India, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union also attended the inaugural meeting as observers.
Countries join by invitation from Trump and normally serve up to three years. Countries that pay more than $1bn in cash in the charter’s first year are exempt from that limit.
Which countries have pledged money?
At the board’s first meeting in Washington, DC, on February 19, Trump announced about $7bn in pledges from nine countries, plus a $10bn US pledge. He did not say what the US money would be used for.
The UAE pledged $1.2bn. Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia pledged $1bn each, with Saudi Arabia saying it would pay over several years. Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Kazakhstan, Morocco, and Uzbekistan also pledged.
What happened to the funding earmarked for Gaza?
At a briefing in New York on September 23, the board said donors had made about $18bn [pdf] in early funding commitments. It said it had called in $280m from donors for the building phase so far, and that most of it remained unspent.
Board of Peace officials previously told the Washington Post that the money couldn’t be spent on projects until Israel allowed international troops or newly-trained Palestinian police to enter Gaza and begin the process of disarming Hamas.
The board puts the cost of rebuilding Gaza at about $71bn, close to the UN’s estimate of $71.5bn, a figure that could rise as more damage is recorded. The board has identified $6bn in projects. It says its six-month recovery plan needs $2.45bn for 66 programmes, plus about $200m in in-kind support.
What does the six-month recovery programme cover?
The 66 programmes are divided across six areas:
- Infrastructure development: 24 programmes
- Human development: 17 programmes
- Peace and security: 11 programmes
- Economic acceleration: 7 programmes
- Digital transformation: 6 programmes
- Legal: 1 programme
Who has pledged to help Gaza?
The Board of Peace highlights five countries helping Gaza’s recovery on the ground. Others have pledged money, but the board has not said how much each has pledged.
- Egypt: Training a civil guard
- Kazakhstan: University scholarships
- Morocco: Disarming fighters and helping them return to civilian life
- Romania: Medical evacuations
- United Arab Emirates: Resources, support and its own programmes

But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026.
The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b.
“Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”.
Israel has continued to occupy and attack parts of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River since March, claiming to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure, while demolishing civilian homes.
On Wednesday, Israel fired artillery shells towards the towns of Baraachit and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). The towns of Rashaf and Sarbine, extending to Wadi al-Hujair, were also targeted. And Israeli earth movers demolished residential homes in the town of Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah and Haddatha.
The United Nations estimates at least 304,500 Lebanese remain internally displaced in the country, down from 1.2 million. Up to 4,500 have been killed in Israeli attacks.
Last month, Hezbollah announced it will pay up to $14,000 to families whose homes were destroyed or made uninhabitable by Israel, as the group accused the government of failing to carry out its duties to help the displaced.
Israel has refused to withdraw from southern Lebanon, citing security concerns connected to the delayed disarmament of Hezbollah and other groups, which the United States and the Lebanese government have insisted on, as part of the trilateral ceasefire framework launched in April.
“Israel will not withdraw from the current lines of these security zones, nor will it redeploy its forces,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that if tensions escalate on the various fronts, “we are fully prepared to seize additional territory”.
Bjerde said that “institutions in Lebanon are very thinly stretched” and the security situation required “very careful planning around where you can start and where you don’t start” to remove rubble and repair infrastructure.
The World Bank projected Lebanon’s economy to shrink by 6.4 percent this year, in its Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor report, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy.
“The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said.
According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than one million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of hunger.
Despite this, Lebanon’s western-backed government insists it is doing all it can, given the circumstances, such as the distribution of approximately $100m in housing loans granted to 1,500 families, according to NNA.
Bjerde said the World Bank needs to be “insistent” and “very close to monitoring on a daily basis” to make sure the work gets done “because you cannot let the people down”, adding that the World Bank wants to see the reconstruction work go more quickly.

articles.title: As UNIFIL winds down, Israeli presence in Lebanon complicates handover process
articles.snippet: If the Lebanese authorities are unable to take physical possession of the positions, the handover could take place on paper only, sources said.
articles.full_text:
BEIRUT — Officials with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) are finalizing an exit plan after 48 years of mission operations along the Blue Line, the demarcation line separating Lebanon and Israel. The process will involve the gradual departure of troops and equipment, and the handover of facilities to Lebanese authorities, amid uncertainty over what comes next.
Following an August 2025 decision by United Nation Security Council (UNSC), peacekeeping operations in southern Lebanon will cease at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, with troops expected to begin withdrawing from the country in the first months of 2027. The process is likely to extend until September 2027, rather than conclude in June as initially projected.
“Midnight is when things change,” UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel said, referring to the last day of the year. “That’s when legally we no longer have a mandate under Resolution 1701.” According to Ardiel, patrols and monitoring activities, as well as the reporting of violations to the Security Council, will continue until the very end.
The peacekeeping force currently counts approximately 7,500 military personnel from several countries around the world deployed on the Lebanese side of the border, with the largest troop contingents provided by Italy and Indonesia.
An average of 1,000 troops are expected to leave each month.
Beginning in January 2027, UNIFIL will start decommissioning positions and carrying out the handover process. “Closing the mission and withdrawing is a logistically complicated process, and it’s done in stages,” Ardiel said.
Troops are set to leave the country with the equipment made available by their respective contributing countries, while UN-owned materiel is likely to be transferred to other UN-led missions or organizations. “Some of it will probably be gifted to the Lebanese authorities,” the spokeswoman said.
The security situation in southern Lebanon remains tense, with Israeli forces occupying approximately 232 square miles of Lebanese territory (nearly 6% of the country) and carrying out daily demolitions and other military operations. This, coupled with the lack of a clear plan for what will follow UNIFIL’s departure, means that some details of the withdrawal plan remain undefined, as the mission waits to see how the situation unfolds on the ground.
The most complicated topic remains the handover of facilities. “Legally, UNIFIL has to return its positions to the Lebanese authorities, but complications arise when those positions are located in areas where Israeli forces are present,” Ardiel explained. According to her, most of these facilities are located in areas where Israeli forces are present, while Lebanese forces remain absent from those same areas to avoid potential clashes.
If the Lebanese authorities are unable to take physical possession of the positions, the handover could take place on paper only, sources said.
Another possible scenario could see the involvement or the expansion of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization (UNTSO), which operates in Lebanon through the Observer Group Lebanon (OGL), a much smaller presence that operates out of UNIFIL positions. However, any decision on the matter rests with the Security Council.
Local administrations in the area hold different views on the withdrawal of the peacekeeping force. While some have expressed security concerns about the end of the mission, others are skeptical about its military role and more worried about the additional economic strain it could place on villages closer to the border.
“[The peacekeepers] didn’t prevent uncontrolled weapons in our area,” said Rabih Rashid, a local official from the southern village of Marjayoun. On the other hand, he added, “socially speaking, they have implemented many projects that have greatly helped people and municipalities.”
Closer to the border, people are exceedingly anxious. “UNIFIL’s withdrawal worries residents and all of us, as it will leave a major security vacuum and expose the region to all kind of possibilities,” said Adam Farhat, mayor of southern village of Chebaa. According to Farhat, the absence of anyone to monitor developments on the ground or hold those responsible for violations to account raises fear of further Israeli expansion.
“This is beyond our power as local administrators, but we are calling on all the relevant authorities to work towards keeping these forces in place and renewing their mandate,” he said.
The Lebanese government has repeatedly called for an extension of UNIFIL’s mandate, while countries such as France and Italy have expressed interest in forming an international coalition to support Lebanon. Following the recent visit to Lebanon by U.S. ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, discussions on the future security arrangements along the Blue Line are expected to intensify in the coming weeks.

articles.title: EU proposes €45 billion Ukraine loan, to be repaid after Russia pays reparations
articles.snippet: The European Commission on Wednesday proposed a new €45 billion ($49.5 billion) loan to Ukraine to help fill a funding gap of €70 billion for next year as Kyiv continues its fight against Russia's 2022 invasion.
articles.full_text:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday proposed a new €45 billion ($49.5 billion) loan to Ukraine to help fill a funding gap of €70 billion for next year as Kyiv continues its fight against Russia’s 2022 invasion.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused by the war.
The planned measure, which requires approval from EU member countries, would come on top of a similar loan of €90 billion to Ukraine agreed by EU leaders at the end of last year to fund Ukraine in 2026 and 2027.
“Five years since the start of this war of aggression, Europe stands united,” von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “We are as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace.”
Kyiv’s other international partners would be expected to provide the rest of the money to fill next year’s funding gap, von der Leyen said.
The Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation European Union, proposed that to up to €25 billion from the new loan could be spent on military aid and up to €20 billion on general budget support.
To finance the loan, the European Commission would borrow on behalf of the EU on international markets, officials said.
Intensified Russian attacks
European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said Ukraine needed additional support because Russia is intensifying attacks on critical infrastructure and disrupting trade, particularly by blocking Black Sea export routes.
“For almost five years, Ukraine has stood guard against the Russian aggression that also threatens our citizens, our territory, and our way of life. Our support gives Ukraine a crucial strategic partner,” he said.
Von der Leyen said she was confident all EU members would back the new loan, even though three – Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia – opted out of the last one.
She said even EU countries that did not favor giving military aid to Ukraine were still committed to supporting Kyiv more generally, so their support for the loan could be attributed to meeting civilian needs.

articles.title: Hanwha transforms ship into floating multi-rocket launcher
articles.snippet: South Korean defense giant Hanwha said it successfully launched missiles from a palletizable multi-pod launcher system at sea.
articles.full_text:
South Korean defense giant Hanwha said it successfully launched missiles from a palletizable multi-pod launcher system at sea on Sunday, demonstrating how heavy maritime strike power has shrunk to the size of shipping containers.
Hanwha Defense USA fired two Chunmoo missiles from a test range vessel operated by the Spaceport Company off the coast of Mississippi, the company announced in a Tuesday release.
The Chunmoo is a self-propelled multiple rocket launcher, designed and produced by Hanwha. Its central asset is its extreme versatility and it can fire an array of different missiles, including munitions with and without precision-guiding systems.
The U.S. Navy has been pushing for containerized weapons systems over the past year and in March, Admiral Daryl Caudle announced a program to shift the Navy toward modular, containerized systems that can fit onto most vessels and are easy to modify and deploy.
Addressing the fleet in April, Caudle announced a new “Containerization Plan” and emphasized that the Navy’s future will focus on adaptable technology that can integrate across multiple domains rather than platforms designed for a single purpose.
“Containerization allows us to decouple payloads from platforms. To rapidly reconfigure forces. To tailor capability to mission. To scale effects across the entire Fleet,” Caudle said in his address. “This is how we emphasize payloads over platforms in practice. It turns every platform into a potential combat node. And every payload into a scalable weapon.”
“If it fits in a container, I want it and I should be able to fight anywhere in the world with it across many, many platforms,” Caudle said.
The demand for containerized systems extends to unmanned sensors and systems, such as unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), or underwater drones.
In March, the Navy chose Anduril to design an unmanned underwater vehicle for its Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform (CAMP) Program based on the design of its Dive-XL vehicle. One of the Dive-XL’s standout features is that it fits neatly into commercial shipping containers, making it easy to transport and deploy.
According to Hanwha, the palletized launcher system it demonstrated on Sunday can be used by both crewed and uncrewed systems. This would mean that autonomous surface vessels could potentially equip multi-rocket launchers previously reserved for ground combat, effectively becoming floating launch pads for heavy firepower.
Kevin Schoonover, Hanwha Defense USA Executive Vice President, said in a statement that Hanwha is responding to the U.S. Navy’s demands to create new modern maritime strike capabilities.
“Hanwha is answering the U.S. Navy’s call to produce and field modern strike capabilities from a maritime platform. By pairing Hanwha’s flagship Chunmoo missile and its palletized platform with next generation crewed and uncrewed vessels, we can deliver capabilities for the Navy at scale and a fraction of the cost of other systems,” he said in the statement.
“The data collected during this test will help shape future distributed maritime operations and expeditionary strike capabilities for both palletized and containerized launcher concepts.”

articles.full_text:
The Trump administration nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve as chief of staff of the Army, according to a Monday congressional notice, moving formally to fill the role left vacant after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April.
LaNeve, also the Army’s vice chief of staff, has been serving as the acting chief of staff in the interim. He needs Senate confirmation to officially take the position.
“He is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield. I cannot think of anyone better to serve as our next Chief of Staff of the Army,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a social media statement regarding LaNeve’s nomination. Telle said he anticipated “working with the Senate” to get LaNeve — and Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans, who would take on vice chief responsibilities — confirmed.
The administration nominated Evans to fill the role of vice chief of staff of the Army, according to another Monday congressional notice.
After former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned in September amid reported tension with Hegseth, the Army has been without Senate-confirmed top uniformed and civilian leadership. Telle has not been officially nominated to fill the Army secretary role.
LaNeve, who formerly served as Hegseth’s military aide, was nominated for the vice chief role before former Vice Chief James Mingus had completed the typical four-year term in the position. Hegseth’s tenure in the Pentagon has been marked by senior leadership shakeups and the firing of over a dozen generals and admirals.
LaNeve has drawn congressional ire for eliminating the 600-member “Unmanned Assault Battalion,” which was created as part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade. He has since sought to reassure industry leaders that the Army is committed to autonomy, changing the name of the command charged with shaping the future force to U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.
Evans is currently serving as director of Army staff in Washington, according to the service. Previously, he was special assistant to the commanding general at Fort Shafter, Hawaii. He also worked as the special operations command chief of staff from 2021 to 2023, and commanded the Special Operations Joint Task Force-Afghanistan from 2020 to 2021.
He was promoted lieutenant general in September of last year and major general in February 2022.
The nominations come after massive Republican losses during midterm elections, which will shift control of the House and Senate to Democrats during the next year’s congressional session.

articles.title: Finland’s Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
articles.snippet: Finnish satellite operator Iceye made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket maker Avio on Tuesday, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defense group.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business.
The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday.
The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.”
Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it.
Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production.
Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs.
An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval.
In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers.
Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.
With material from Reuters by Giulia Segreti and Essi Lehto.

articles.title: Lithuanian president says US troop rotations will continue beyond latest deployment
articles.snippet: Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that U.S. troop rotations in the country would continue beyond the current nine-month deployment.
articles.full_text:
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on Monday that U.S. troop rotations in Lithuania would continue beyond the current nine-month deployment, speaking at a ceremony marking the arrival of the latest two U.S. battalions.
Washington first deployed troops to Lithuania, a NATO member bordering Russia and Belarus, in 2014 after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.
Since 2019, it had maintained an armoured battalion of about 1,000 troops on overlapping rotations until the Pentagon paused it earlier this year pending a force posture review.
At the Pabrade military base near the Belarusian border, Nauseda said: “As far as I know, this is not a one-off or a temporary rotation. There is a certain rotation plan extending into the future.”
The U.S. Embassy in Lithuania did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
U.S. Ambassador Kara McDonald, speaking at the same ceremony, did not directly comment on Nauseda’s remarks but described the deployment as “a continuation of rotations” that have taken place since 2014.
“Our purpose here is very clear,” she told reporters. “It is a defensive purpose to project deterrence, to maintain readiness, to stand shoulder to shoulder with our allies. This very much is peace through strength, and this is how we preserve peace.”
Lithuania has proposed expanding U.S. presence or making it permanent and has offered to cover the costs.
President Donald Trump told reporters last month his administration would “certainly look at” Lithuania’s request.
Lithuania has tripled defense spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and is NATO’s biggest defense spender this year by share of gross domestic product at 5.33%.
Germany is due to station a combat-ready army brigade of about 5,000 troops in Lithuania by the end of next year as a deterrent to Russia.

articles.title: Britain has the frigate the US needs, and Americans should build it: UK minister
articles.snippet: In a new op-ed, Britain’s Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry makes the case that the US should procure a UK frigate design and produce it in America.
articles.full_text:
For more than a century, British and American forces have fought side-by-side to defend freedom and democracy around the world. Together with our other allies, we are the most formidable force in history when it comes to safeguarding our shared values and shared interests. Our combined capabilities are second to none.
Driving those capabilities is the United States Navy — the most powerful military machine ever put to sea. President Donald Trump understands this, which is why he has set about rebuilding America’s shipbuilding base. He recognizes that maritime power rests on industrial power. Ships cannot be conjured up in a crisis if the yards, the trained workforce and the supply chains are not already there. As we are learning in Britain, rebuilding our maritime industry is not only a defense imperative, it is an economic and strategic one.
As the US rebuilds its naval might, there is one hole that stands out: a lack of dedicated frigates in service. The workhorses of any navy, frigates escort carriers, protect shipping lanes, hunt submarines, and shoot down missiles and drones. This frees up the destroyers and aircraft carriers to carry out the toughest tasks.
As a trusted partner, the United Kingdom can help the president’s initiative, with an offer that fits his agenda: an American frigate, built by Americans, for the US Navy.
What we can do is provide an off-the-shelf design based on the Arrowhead 140 by UK company Babcock International. The design is proven as the basis of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates currently being built in Scotland, the home of the president’s mother’s family — it might be fitting for an American version to carry the name of the “MacLeod” frigate in honor of that legacy.
At around 150 yards and 6,000 tons, the Arrowhead 140 is a flexible and affordable vessel that can take on a wide range of tasks, from air defense to maritime security, with the capacity to deploy for long periods in remote regions. And because it starts from a proven design rather than a blank sheet of paper, it carries far less risk than a new program.
Crucially, any new frigate would be an all-American ship. The US would set the requirements, choose its weapons, sensors and communications, and keep sovereign control of upgrades and configuration. And the benefits would be felt in American communities. Construction in US shipyards would create and sustain skilled jobs for welders, engineers and apprentices, and open up opportunities for US suppliers.
The design simply offers a ready-made starting point. We would also share our modern shipbuilding know-how, including production processes, robotics and workforce training, to strengthen American capacity for the long term.
Stronger shipyards mean stronger deterrence, and greater resilience for both our nations. As the son of a submariner, I know it is not just those who wear the uniform, it is those in industry who keep us safe.
These days, it is not enough for an alliance to mobilize its armies; we must also be able to mobilize our industries. An American frigate built to a British design is proof that stronger domestic industries and deeper integration between trusted partners are not contradictory. The defining test is not who designed this and who made that. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it.
Already, the UK’s active foreign military sales portfolio with the US exceeds $11 billion. British industry produces around 15 percent of each F-35 through more than 100 UK Tier-1 suppliers, supporting over 20,000 jobs. Through AUKUS, US investment in its submarine industrial base is matched by substantial British investment in our Defence Nuclear Enterprise.
So, this is not a leap into the unknown. Babcock, who already have long-standing partnerships with American industry, including with Huntington Ingalls Industries and Lockheed Martin, have submitted an expression of interest to the Department of War and His Majesty’s Government in the UK is fully behind it.
Underpinning all this is trust. Our militaries train together, deploy together and share intelligence at a level no other nations can match. Our capabilities are strengthened by our ability to operate alongside each other. But interoperability cannot be bolted on later. Building a frigate that Royal Navy and US Navy sailors can operate, maintain and upgrade together would be a practical expression of our deep bond in an increasingly uncertain world.
America needs frigates. Britain has a proven design, a trusted industrial partner and a shared commitment to our steadfast alliance.
So, when America is looking at which ally to work with on its new frigate, I encourage the White House to look at the nation of the Mayflower, of Winston Churchill, a nation which has stood alongside the US Navy in the Atlantic and Pacific for generations.
Our partnership has always been built on trust, and we are ready to deliver again.
Luke Pollard MP is the UK Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry.

articles.title: From mine to magnet: What defense buyers need to verify before 2027
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] January’s expanded magnet-sourcing restrictions will require defense contractors to trace each finished magnet back to its raw materials and document how and where it was produced.
articles.full_text:
The Army has acknowledged the difficulty. In Breaking Defense’s October 15 reporting, Liz Miranda, Army Materiel Command’s executive deputy to the commanding general, said the White House directive to map supply chains down to the raw-material level “is no easy task.”
For magnet buyers, that challenge combines sourcing, manufacturing, and qualifications into the same conversation. A supplier must demonstrate the required magnetic properties, support delivery commitments, and provide the necessary proof of the material pathway behind its products.
Evolution Metals & Technologies, known as EM&T, is addressing that challenge through its established magnet manufacturing operations in South Korea, additional feedstock commitments, and an expansion now underway. The company has also announced plans to develop U.S. manufacturing and critical materials recovery capabilities, including recycling end-of-life magnets to recover materials for new production and support supply chains aligned with applicable U.S. sourcing requirements.
The Sourcing Challenge Reaches Beyond the Factory
Beginning January 1, 2027, the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) 252.225-7052 expands restrictions for covered contract deliveries to include materials mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China, Russia, North Korea or Iran.
For neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the restriction extends from mining neodymium, iron and boron through finished magnet production. Samarium-cobalt magnets face expanded supply-chain restrictions as well, subject to applicable exceptions.
EM&T Builds its Material Supply Position
EM&T already manufactures and sells bonded and sintered magnets. Its October 28 and 29 announcements describe eight customer-certified high-performance sintered magnet grades, providing an established product foundation for its expansion.
On October 29, 2026, EM&T reported securing approximately 754 metric tons of neodymium metal sourced outside China, approximately 42 metric tons delivered to Pohang, 72 metric tons pending shipment through March 2027 and 640 metric tons committed through the end of 2027. The committed portion includes a 600-metric-ton Senri Trading contract.
For procurement teams, those categories make the supply position clear. Received inventory supports near-term production planning; committed volumes give visibility into supply through 2027.
EM&T has sourced some materials from China for its broader commercial business. For defense applications, the company intends to supply magnets that meet the expanded requirements through a documented sourcing pathway, with origin and processing history tied to each production lot.
Connecting Material Origins with Product Qualification
“Defense customers need confidence in both the magnet’s performance and the materials behind it,” said David Wilcox, Executive Chairman of the Board of Evolution Metals & Technologies. “That requires connecting origin documentation and processing history to the production lot, while demonstrating that the finished magnet meets the application’s magnetic, dimensional and coating requirements.”
“We already produce N42SH commercially, a grade the Army identifies as acceptable for its small-drone motor requirement. Our capability statement proposes a staged qualification process supported by auditable mine-to-magnet traceability for each production lot. Our focus is demonstrating how our manufacturing capabilities and sourcing documentation can meet the customer’s specific requirements.”
Pohang Expansion Advances Toward Higher Production Capacity
On October 28, 2026, EM&T announced delivery of all 57 containers of additional ULVAC production equipment to its Pohang facility, where commissioning is underway. Once installed and commissioned, the expansion is expected to increase total annual magnet capacity from approximately 1,000 to 10,000 metric tons, including approximately 6,000 metric tons of high-performance sintered magnets.
The expansion builds upon an existing manufacturing business with customer-qualified magnet grades and disclosed material commitments. Installation, commissioning and a controlled production ramp will bring the additional capacity into service, expanding EM&T’s ability to support and adhere to the demands from domestic buyers.
With manufacturing in South Korea and a planned U.S. expansion, EM&T is developing both allied and domestic production options for defense contractors, integrators and strategic materials partners. Interested organizations can request an initial sourcing and qualification discussion through EM&T’s investor relations website.
EM&T will host its Korea Flagship Expansion Ribbon-Cutting Ceremony on Thursday, December 17, 2026, at its Pohang facility. Register at evolution-metals.com/rsvp.

articles.title: Lawmakers challenge Trump’s push to bring steam catapults back to Ford-class carriers
articles.snippet: The bipartisan pushback came during Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing, where senators questioned the cost and capability trade-offs of returning future Ford-class carriers to steam-powered catapults.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle urged Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao to reconsider plans to return to steam catapults for the Ford-class aircraft carriers, following President Donald Trump’s instructions in August to reinstate the technology.
“Secretary Cao, returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that,” Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said today during Cao’s confirmation hearing to become secretary of the Navy.
The Ford class employs the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, or EMALS, which uses electromagnetic energy rather than steam to launch aircraft from the flight deck. In August, Trump issued a National Security Presidential Memorandum that directed the Navy to instead equip Ford-class aircraft carriers with traditional steam-powered catapults and hydraulic aircraft elevators, similar to those on Nimitz-class carriers. The directive would apply to ships such as the Doris Miller, currently under construction at HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding.
Trump has long criticized EMALS and indicated last year he would direct the Navy to return to steam. In the August memo, he argued that overly complex ship designs and repeated changes have contributed to shipbuilding cost increases, delays and cancellations. He called on the Navy to prioritize “proven, reliable, and affordable technologies and ship designs.”
Critics argue that returning to steam would add costs and complexity while reverting to older technology on a carrier class designed around EMALS. Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have pushed back on the plans, as well.
Prior to Wicker’s comments, Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told Cao that he had recently visited the Ford and spoken with sailors who were “very complimentary” of EMALS. Asked whether the Navy should return to steam catapults, Cao said EMALS and the electromagnetic elevators outfitted on the Ford are contributing to carrier delays.
But Kaine warned that reverting to steam would drive up costs with “diminished capacity.”
“And so, just because the president directed it, I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford in deciding before you decide to go down a path that will be more expensive and also less capable,” he said.
Iran Conflict and Transparency
Trump announced in September that he would nominate Cao to serve as secretary of the Navy. Cao has led the service in an acting capacity since April, when former Navy Secretary John Phelan was ousted by the Trump administration and Cao — then the Navy’s undersecretary — assumed the role.
During his confirmation hearing, Cao faced questions about the impact of the conflict with Iran and the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln’s extended deployment from November 2025 to October 2026 — including quality-of-life issues and eight suicide attempts during that period.
Pressed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-NY, on his characterization of the incidents as “suicide mitigations,” Cao pointed to his own deployment experience and said he understood the strain facing sailors.
“I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand said. “If it was your son or your daughter, would you be minimizing and saying, ‘Well, there was mitigation?’ I don’t think you would. I think your response is inhumane. I think it’s inadequate. I don’t think it understands the stress and strain that these men and women are on because of these poor conditions.”
Cao also pledged to include Democrats in classified congressional briefings after Sen. Mike Rounds, R-SD, raised concerns about their exclusion from previous hearings and argued that it would make approving funding and policy changes difficult.
Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., meanwhile, questioned whether Cao had warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about the strain the Iran conflict was placing on the Navy. Cao responded that Hegseth “knows my stance on our readiness and the strain it takes on our sailors.”
“I cannot vote for you because you’re going to be another yes man,” Duckworth said.
On the other side of the aisle, Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., voiced support for Cao, saying it was “fundamentally important” to have a confirmed Navy secretary for the next two years and lauded Cao for his efforts supporting Naval Support Activity Crane in Indiana.
Cao enlisted in the Navy as a seaman recruit in 1989, and later graduated from the US Naval Academy in 1996. He served more than 20 years as a naval officer before retiring in 2021 from the service as a captain.
Military retirees must have been retired for at least seven years to serve as a service secretary, meaning Cao will need waivers from both the House and Senate to be confirmed.
